description: A young Fool in a beautiful dress clutches a small white flower — symbol of purity and spirit. Her staff, which should represent strength, is used instead to lightly hook her little bundle. Eyes closed, she steps lightly and confidently forward, unaware of the cliff ahead. Her little dog trots beside her as if warning her of danger at her feet, yet she walks on, carefree and unshaken. This optimistic, radiant soul sets out on a journey entirely her own.

A magnificently dressed Magician conjures with quiet confidence. Her left hand holds a book of spells; her right, a wand. The infinity symbol above her head is the source of her energy, and her braids and flowers float suspended in the air by magic's grace. On the table before her rest the four elements: the Cup of water, the Wand of fire, the Sword of air, and the Pentacle of earth — all four mastered and wielded with equal ease.

A serene, composed High Priestess sits at the center, cradling a scroll of wisdom in her hands. The scroll's half-hidden state hints at deeper layers of knowing yet to be revealed. Her lunar crown and white robes speak of purity; the moon at her feet, of wisdom. To either side stand pillars of black and white — the black inscribed with B for Boaz, meaning "to establish," the white with J for Jachin, meaning "inner strength" — together forming the Pillars of Truth, the balance of duality, the intelligence of the unconscious.

A radiant Empress full of maternal warmth leans back on her couch with a gentle smile. Her crown holds twelve stars for the twelve signs of the zodiac; her right hand bears a scepter of authority; her gown is dotted with pomegranate motifs, symbols of fertility. A pillow bearing the Venus symbol (♀) rests beside her. Plants and flowers surround her in abundance, and even the curtains behind her are embroidered with wheat sheaves — the earth in full, fruitful bloom.

A commanding Emperor sits upon his throne, crowned with authority, robed in red. One hand grips an orb; the other holds an ankh scepter, symbol of the life force. Four ram heads are carved into his throne, echoing Aries in astrology. The rolling mountains behind him speak of great challenges and trials he has faced and endured. He is not skilled at expressing emotion and has learned to keep his feelings carefully concealed beneath that regal composure.

The Hierophant stands before his disciples, right hand raised toward heaven in blessing, left hand clasping a staff in the shape of a cross — the mark of the divine. His triple crown represents the three tiers of body, mind, and spirit. His two followers listen intently, hungry to be guided, completed, and awakened through his teachings. Between them rest two keys, symbols of the wisdom that joins inner and outer worlds, unlocking the doors of mystery and enlightenment.

Two lovers embrace. Behind them, twelve flames burn for the twelve signs of the zodiac — the fire of desire. A tree of wisdom bears five fruits, representing the five senses; a serpent of temptation coils nearby as if luring them toward falling. In the distance, the masculine mountain and the nearby feminine water express a state of harmonious balance — yin and yang, energies aligned in dynamic accord.

A spirited female warrior drives a chariot pulled by two bears — one black, one white — emblems of yin-yang balance and the wild, barely-tameable forces of emotion and desire. The warrior inside wears armor, holds a staff of will and strength, and wears a laurel crown of victory. She holds no reins; sheer willpower keeps the two beasts in check. She seems to be both defending the walled city at her back and leaving its material concerns behind, moving forward on a journey of the spirit.

A small, graceful girl in a layered gown moves with the elegance of a dancer on a piano. The ribbons woven into her hair and the flowers embroidered on her dress speak of noble purity and gentleness. Above her head, an infinity symbol declares that her power has no limit. She reaches out and gently strokes the great lion before her; it lies docile, head tilted toward her, already tamed. The lion is human instinct, now brought to heel by wisdom and by a spirit that rises higher.

A barefoot girl stands on a mountaintop in deep contemplation, not another soul in sight. One hand lifts a lantern of truth high overhead — inside it glows a six-pointed star, its light illuminating the path to wisdom. In her other hand she holds a staff that has appeared before in the Fool, the Magician, and the Chariot — always an instrument of self-inquiry, a medium for the inward search.

Here the Wheel of Fortune is encircled by the Tree of Life. On its outer ring are carved the letters T-A-R-O and the Hebrew name YHVH for Jehovah; the inner ring holds four alchemical symbols. Above the tree sits a sphinx; below, Anubis in jackal form — the ascending soul and the descending fall. At the four corners stand the eagle (Scorpio/water), the lion (Leo/fire), the bull (Taurus/earth), and the man (Aquarius/air), each governing an element and holding sway over the world's ceaseless change. The Wheel turns and turns — the world is nothing if not unpredictable.

A woman sits upright on a stone bench, right hand raising a sword perfectly straight — not tilted left or right, the emblem of impartiality. In her left hand, scales: the symbol of Libra. Her eyes are closed, her expression austere, untouched by any external circumstance. The two pillars at her sides speak of positive and negative forces held in exact balance.

A woman hangs inverted with her hands behind her back, forming a triangle with her body. Her crossed legs make a cross; cross and triangle together form an alchemical symbol of base desire transmuted into higher soul — a figure of baptism, sacrifice, devotion, and the readiness to begin a new and more elevated life. Light radiates from around her, the glow of wisdom and the evolution of spirit.

Death rides a white horse, crowned with feathers and bearing the rose-cross banner. Four figures appear: a king crushed beneath the hooves for resisting; a pope with hands clasped in reverence; a woman who has fainted or cannot bear to look; a child, innocent of death, who only stares with curiosity. Together they proclaim that death makes no exception for age, gender, or rank. A river flows in the distance — the unceasing cycle of life. Behind the mountains, a rising light speaks of hope and new birth, as if to say: death is never the end.

A long-haired girl in a beautiful gown has butterfly wings on her back — emblems of transformation. On her chest, a square within a triangle merges spirit and animal nature, earth element and fire element together, the spirit rising from the body. Her right foot steps into a pond of the unconscious; her left stands on the stone shore of conscious awareness. She pours water between two cups held in each hand, an endless back-and-forth that sustains dynamic equilibrium between yin and yang. Light blazes from a distant mountaintop, signaling that this card has transcended the fear Death brought before it. The whole card breathes peace — a quiet assurance that new life follows death.

A man and a woman, cursed and shackled, have become the Devil's servants. This is Adam and Eve at their origins: Eve's tail is the forbidden fruit of the Tree of Knowledge; Adam's tail bears the flame of the Tree of Life. They ate the fruit in a moment of temptation and were cast into darkness. The Devil represents the seduction of the material world and desire — the relentless pursuit of status and wealth, and the sinking into hunger for things both physical and spiritual.

A tall tower at the summit of a mountain is struck by lightning and shattered. Two figures fall headfirst from its heights. The crown is about to topple from the blow. Twenty-two sparks scatter to either side, one for each of the Major Arcana. The Tower bears heaven's punishment: the tower itself symbolizes the material, the crown symbolizes dominion and achievement — and at the fatal stroke, all of it is wiped away. Lightning is the language of divine reckoning, and catastrophe that strikes without warning heralds a period of deep darkness.

A golden-haired girl crowned with flowers stands with her left foot on the ground of conscious awareness and her right foot in the pool of the unconscious. She holds a jug in each hand — both filled with the water of life. Her right jug pours into the pool, sending out ripples; her left pours onto the earth, splitting into five streams for the five human senses, one of which flows back to replenish the spring of the unconscious. Flowers bloom behind her; a bird of wisdom soars overhead — the creator of all art. Behind her stretches a vast flowering meadow and a mountain range; in the sky shines one enormous gold star, with seven smaller eight-pointed stars arrayed around it.

A full moon hangs in the night sky, and in its face appears a woman — eyes closed, brow furrowed, her expression a portrait of confusion and unease. Below stand a white pet dog and a wild black wolf, both startled and facing the moon, representing the tamed inner world and the untamed beast within. At the bottom, a crab creeps from the water onto land, carrying an anxiety deeper even than fear or instinct. The winding, seemingly endless path stretching ahead stands for unknown dangers, deepening the Moon's pervading sense of disorientation and dread.

A golden-haired child wearing a floral wreath embodies the vitality of new life. Four sunflowers on the surrounding wall represent the four elements — and they all face the child rather than the sun, suggesting this child's energy has already surpassed the sun above. The child rides bareback, no reins needed: pure energy in full, effortless command. The red banner in the child's hand is the symbol of action; the sun in the background is the source of all life.

An angel blows a trumpet from the sky, and the music has the power to liberate humanity from the constraints of the material world, healing body and soul alike. Below the angel lies a sea representing the unconscious; floating on it are many coffins bearing people — the coffins symbolize the old patterns of the material world. New flowers have already sprouted inside them, while those in the distance are still gray. A man in the foreground, symbol of the conscious mind, gazes up at the angel with quiet awe; a woman, symbol of the unconscious, stretches out both arms and welcomes the angel's call with open generosity; a child, symbol of the reborn self, has its back to us.

A dancer of fluid grace moves within a laurel wreath — symbol of victory. Clothed in a gown of nobility and holiness, she bears gossamer butterfly wings whose lightness declares that her transformation is complete and whole. She holds two wands with the gentlest touch — the forces of evolution and involution. The oval shape she moves within, nearly a zero, signals the close of this cycle and the imminent arrival of the next — the Fool, and a new round of becoming. At the top and bottom of the wreath sit two infinity symbols, emblems of the boundless and eternal. The four creatures at the corners — eagle, lion, bull, and man — appeared once in the Wheel of Fortune with books in hand, gathering knowledge; now, in the World, they complete their purpose.

Two hands reach out from the clouds and take hold of a staff adorned with leaves and a gleaming jewel. The grip is confident and easy, hinting at vitality and enthusiasm. Far off, a high mountain marks the destination — the possibility of success.

High on a mountain, a girl stands tall, chest lifted, eyes closed in thought — planning for the future, and quietly signaling that the present is not enough. A bold, successful idea or decision is already forming in her mind. She holds two wands; the readiness to act is matched by the awareness of two distinct paths she might take.

A merchant woman stands at a mountain summit and gazes out over the distant sea, drawn toward horizons that seem to call for action. Three wands are in her hands. She is clearly a visionary leader: the higher you climb, the farther you see — and the farther you see, the more forward-looking your choices become.

Four great pillars, tall as wands, rise from the earth, draped with victory banners and festive lights. In the foreground, a beautiful woman holds a sparkling gem and dances with easy, buoyant steps — celebrating something. Fireworks bloom overhead. The whole scene is drenched in joy, a picture of harmony and delight.

Under the influence of the fire element, five people in the open wild each clutch a staff. They all hold different views; five wands point in five different directions. Each person is convinced their way is best. No one listens to anyone else. The struggle continues, locked and chaotic, with no end in sight.

An armored knight, laurel crown on her head, rides home in triumph on a black horse. The wands all around represent both the crowds who support her and the banner of her victory. The wand held by the rider is a trophy in itself. The hard fight is behind her; now she can ride with head held high and receive the crowd's acclamation and glory.

A girl stands at ease on a hillside, one hand raising a wand. The six wands advancing from below seem unlikely to seriously shake her position. She will overcome these challenges in the end — because though she fights alone, she stands on higher ground, and that advantage matters. The Seven of Wands is about the success that comes through sheer, unyielding persistence.

An angel draws a bow; a wand is about to fly. Seven more magic staffs move through the air in perfect formation, swift and unified. The tips point downward, about to reach the earth — nothing can stop them. They may signal the arrival of something new. The speed of the Eight of Wands reflects a moment when obstacles are few and action flows freely.

A wounded female warrior holds tight to her wand; eight more wands stand upright behind her, barring her path. Her head and hands are wrapped in bandages — still healing, not yet whole. Yet she is not afraid. Her posture is taut and alert, showing her vigilance, her stubbornness, and the quiet iron in her will.

A figure stands in a posture of offering, arms spread wide, and ten wand-candles press down heavily upon her — a suffocating, breathless weight. There are many reasons for this overload: inability to refuse, poor planning, taking on too many things at once. The burden is usually not the environment's doing — it comes from her own nature, her own choices, until she buckles under the strain. And yet, because she carries a sense of duty and belief, she does not give up. She takes it all on alone.

The Page of Wands props a staff on the ground, face turned toward it, dressed in bright casual colors that carry a frank, lively energy. In the distance stretch a desert, a pyramid, and a camel traveling far — all emblems of the fire element.

The Knight of Wands rides with open confidence, holding a wand. A fire lizard pattern decorates her bright yellow clothing, though the mouth and tail do not connect — a sign of unfinished action or an incomplete plan. Compared to the King, this Knight has only just begun the adventure. The red cloak is the heat of a fiery nature; the galloping horse is the swiftness of action.

The Queen of Wands wears a crown of leaves and flowers and sits on her throne with sure, settled confidence. Sunflowers — symbols of light and joy — bloom behind her. Her right hand holds a wand; a lion's canopy on the throne symbolizes the inner strength that can hold the instinctive self in check. At her feet, a black cat keeps watch, guardian of inspiration and intuition.

The King holds his wand in his right hand and sits on his throne with complete assurance — lions and lizards adorn it, the lions embodying the fire character. The fire lizard motif, half-joined on the Knight's garment, is now fully joined on the King's throne — the sign of a craft perfected. Fiery red hair and crimson robe edges declare his passionate nature. A fire-breathing lizard stands sentinel at his side.

A white dove descends from above and drops a sacred wafer — symbol of Christ's body — into a golden cup, representing the soul entering the material world. Five streams of water flow out, standing for the five human senses. Water lilies grow in the pool below, suited to deep water, suggesting the emotional well runs full and deep. A hand cradles the cup with care: love requires tender, attentive tending.

A beautifully dressed man and woman bow their heads slightly toward one another, each raising a cup in greeting. Behind them, an arch of connection stands open, wound with ribbons and vines. Between them floats a lion-headed staff entwined by two serpents: the lion's head and wings embody love and beauty; the caduceus-like serpents represent communication and the flow of exchange.

A celebration supper: the red curtains are drawn back, red candles flicker, and three dear friends, wearing flower wreaths and raising their cups, talk and laugh about all the delights and absurdities life has put in their path. The moment of reunion is always something special — may every happiness linger on in their faces forever.

A girl leans against a great tree, knees pulled to her chest in a gesture of self-protection. Three cups on the ground represent past experiences; a cup in the air represents a new opportunity. But her eyes are fixed on the middle distance, and the floating cup goes unseen. Contemplation has turned inward — or, perhaps, into avoidance.

A cloaked and masked figure bows their head in grief over three overturned cups, heavy with dejection. Under an ashen sky, a river flows unhurried. The house in the distance stands for stability and continuity — she is neither alone nor empty-handed. The house is still there. Two cups remain upright behind her. Whenever she is ready, she can pick them up and set out again.

In a courtyard, a boy holds out a cup full of flowers to a girl, as if confiding something long held close. Five more cups brimming with blossoms surround them — the scene calls up the sweet, untroubled innocence of childhood memories.

In a cloud-filled half-sky, seven cups drift with different contents inside each. Below the clouds, clasped hands reach upward — dreaming, or yearning for something just out of reach. The Seven of Cups is the non-material layer of life: dreams, fantasies, daydreams. The cups hold a castle (adventure), jewels (wealth), a laurel crown (victory), a dragon (temptation — or fear), a human head, a glowing shrouded figure (the self), and a serpent (wisdom — or envy).

A beautiful girl leans on her staff and prepares to leave behind the eight cups she has labored to collect, setting out to find the empty ninth. The forest in the distance may mean a hard road ahead, but she shows no sign of hesitating. The Eight of Cups speaks of abandonment — breaking with the familiar through an act of will.

An elegantly dressed woman stands at ease beneath her own tree. Nine cups grow on the lush, emotion-laden tree behind her. Her expression makes it plain: she is deeply satisfied with where she is. There is a simple, unadorned happiness here — pure contentment, a calm pleasure in the accomplishments that have already been gathered.

A family of three is enjoying beautiful time together. The parents lean into each other with warmth and closeness; their child plays joyfully nearby. Vivid flowers, lush plants, and butterflies in flight all around them paint a scene of perfect harmony. Ten cups arc across the sky — the Ten of Cups is a card of joy and sharing, contentment and delight radiating in all directions. Happiness spreads freely to everyone you love.

A Page of Cups stands at the edge of a rolling sea, dressed in beautiful garments, one hand on the hip and a smile on the face — a warm and friendly presence. A fish leaps from the cup held in the other hand. The fish represents imagination, hinting that this Page possesses an extraordinary inner world of creative vision.

Unlike the other court knights, the Knight of Cups rides a white horse that moves with grace and refinement — dashing and gentlemanly, much like its rider. The Knight raises the cup high; the elaborate imagery throughout the card speaks of imagination, creativity, and the life of the spirit.

The Queen of Cups sits on her throne by the sea, gazing with tenderness at the cup she holds. Rich in the water element, she embodies heightened spiritual sensitivity and exquisitely attuned emotional perception.

On a surging sea, the King sits upon his throne, a fish tail peeking out from beneath his robes. Behind him the waves may swell and crash, but the King meets it all with unshaken calm. His success is a blend of imagination, discipline, and steadfast persistence. That steady gaze means self-mastery — and self-mastery is what allows him to succeed, again and again.

A razor-sharp sword pierces a crown; green plants trail down from the crown above, signifying that the mind can see through the physical world to what lies beneath. A beautiful hand reaches out from the clouds and takes hold of the blade. Far off, mist and water move on currents of wind. The double-edged sword stands straight and true — the balanced, neutral force of pure reason.

Clouds roil along the horizon; hidden rocks lurk beneath the sea's surface — the outer world mirrors a turbulent inner life. A woman in an elaborate gown holds two swords, one blade aimed in each direction — a posture of resistance and inner conflict. Her eyes are covered by a winged helmet, representing avoidance of the truths or causes she fears most. One side avoids reality; the other pulls in the opposite direction; the result is impasse — refusal to decide, and the stalemate that comes with it.

In a stormy night thick with clouds and driving rain, flowers and raindrops fall on the wind. A blindfolded girl holds her own vivid red heart against her chest, and three sharp swords pierce it without mercy. This is a card whose pain and grief make themselves felt immediately and unmistakably.

Three swords hang from a rack; a female warrior rests in a half-reclined position beneath them. She hasn't yet removed her armor, and her sword lies close at hand — this is a short rest, not a retreat. She could rise ready for battle at any moment.

A woman with a self-satisfied smile stands holding three swords; two more lie beside her as though they are all trophies she has taken. Behind her stand two unhappy-looking women who appear to be the former owners of those swords. From their expressions and posture, they are not about to let this go quietly. This victory may not be as complete as the winner imagines.

Six swords — symbols of wounds — stand planted in a boat. The woman onboard gazes with sorrow, oar in hand, preparing to row away from this mournful stretch of water. If she pulled the swords out, the holes they leave would sink the boat beyond doubt. The water on this side is rough, but if she can only leave, she will find a calmer lake waiting ahead — and healing works the same way: say goodbye to the past, and go to meet what comes next.

A masked woman dressed in black for a night raid steals away with five swords under cover of surprise, radiating quiet confidence. The two swords left on the ground were simply too many to carry — a sign that this venture carries real risk. Her black clothing says she lacks the power to confront her enemy openly, and so resorts to stealth and cunning, achieving her purpose through deception rather than direct force.

A woman stands blindfolded and bound at the waist, trapped among eight planted swords. In the distance, a manor castle perches on a cliff face — the symbol of the authority that holds her. Escape seems impossibly difficult; she appears to stand alone. But her feet are not tied. The swords do not form a complete cage. There is no guard in sight. One step forward, one act of will, and she is free.

A girl drifts downward through the air, falling as if into a dream of strange, unsettling absurdity — like Alice tumbling into Wonderland. Below is the canopy of a bed, but nine swords lie across the space in between, making the descent through them treacherous. Sleep is not so easily found here. The sharp blades press in with a suffocating weight, building a feeling of absolute despair.

Ten swords plunge cruelly into the body of a woman who has burned down to ash; blood-red flows downward. All life seems to have left her. Far off, the sky is pitch black, bearing down heavily; clouds scatter on the wind in a desolate, hopeless quiet. And yet, at the very edge of the horizon, a faint yellow-green glow has appeared. Even the darkest hour of a life must eventually pass.

The Page of Swords is a quick-minded young person, curiosity always running ahead. One hand grips a sword; the face turns toward what is coming. The trees in the distance and the grass underfoot are all stirred and bent by the wind.

The Knight of Swords has a calm, serious face — and a head of vivid red hair, emblem of the impulsiveness that runs beneath. She wears full armor, holds her sword, rides hard, and moves forward without hesitation. Clouds and plants around her are swept into the shapes the wind makes as it rushes past.

The Queen of Swords is crowned, and the butterfly pattern on her ears speaks of the soul and the element of air. She looks at the upright sword she holds — blade straight and true, a sign that she can cut through illusion and see clearly, blessed with exceptional perception, keen intelligence, an active mind, calm composure, and impartial justice.

A handsome blond King of Swords sits on his throne in grave dignity, eyes closed in contemplation. His right hand holds a sword whose tip tilts slightly to the right — toward action. His left hand wears a ring of authority. Butterfly motifs decorate his throne, symbols of the soul and the air element. In the sky above, the wind tears the clouds apart.

A hand reaches from the clouds and holds a single coin. Behind it, a garden dense with plants and flowers suggests that the Ace of Pentacles is not merely about material wealth — its meaning reaches into the realm of the spirit as well. Nature thrives and multiplies around it: in the practical spirit of the Pentacles suit, whatever you invest — money, time, effort — will return to you with great abundance.

On a stage, a masked dancer juggles two coins, a figure-eight ribbon looping around each. The dramatically shifting sea depicted in the backdrop symbolizes the ups and downs of financial affairs — and, more broadly, the fluctuations of emotion and the many moving currents of a life.

Three people huddle together to plan a home's interior — one is tasked with painting three pentacle motifs in the skylight, one with the architectural drawings, one with thinking through the execution. Each has her role; together the collaboration runs smoothly. From the intensity of their discussion, it is clear they are enjoying the work.

A woman wearing a crown sits on a treasure chest. One coin rests in her crown; another is cradled in her hands with great care; two more are pressed beneath her feet. She is terrified of losing even a fraction of what she owns. Behind her rises a prosperous castle.

In a world of ice and snow, two beggars trudge forward, limping with exhaustion, their clothing in tatters. They pass a church — symbol of shelter for both body and spirit — but do not look up. Hunger and cold drive them onward without pause.

A wealthy patron stands on higher ground, dispensing charity to two supplicants below. The scales of fairness sit before him — yet the situation is his to control, and the pentacles on either side are, in truth, out of balance.

A farmer leans on her spade to rest, expression satisfied, eyes taking in the abundant harvest growing before her. From the scene, it is clear the labor has already begun to bear fruit. She is a little tired now and needs a moment's rest — and a chance to think about where to go from here.

A blacksmith in richly patterned traditional dress works at her bench, striking a coin with her hammer — unhurried, focused, diligent. A row of completed coins is laid out before her, each one representing another step of steady work, another increment of accumulated skill and wealth.

A beautifully dressed woman stands inside her luxurious home; behind her, cabinets full of carefully tended wealth. She holds a small bird in one hand with easy confidence — an image of independence, composure, and self-possessed strength. Pentacles are scattered around her, emblems of material achievement and the pleasures it affords.

In a courtyard, three generations of a family share the warmth of togetherness. From their dress and the beauty of their surroundings, it is plain that this is a family of considerable means — and it is clearly even more traditional and prosperous than what is depicted in the Ten of Cups.

The Page of Pentacles stands in a wide green field, holding a coin raised high, eyes fixed on it with focused, studious attention — ready to examine, to learn, to master. The whole scene is lush with growing green.

The Knight of Pentacles sits upright on a black horse, studying the coin in his hand with careful scrutiny. The black horse stands perfectly still — the only mount among the four Knights that is stationary — a reflection of the Knight's cautious, methodical, grounded approach.

The Queen of Pentacles holds her coin in both hands, seated on her throne with a posture of quiet warmth. She is dressed in the most opulent of furs. The trees behind her are dense with foliage. The whole scene breathes a deep serenity — a sense of abundant resources and quiet, established prosperity.

The King of Pentacles is a ruler who has earned his success. He sits on his throne with full confidence; everything lies within his command. His robes are splendid; vines and green leaves climb across him and around him; behind him rise the towers and buildings of a magnificent city — testament to the flourishing life of all who live under his stewardship.
